title: Five objects
hook: a shelf in five things: image, lamp, flower, bell, water

segments.voice: Yesterday, 108: your first full round on the mala. Your line was 108 is enough. Did you finish one thing and stop? This week, the practice gets a home. Literally. Day one hundred eleven.

In many Hindu homes, somewhere, there's a small shrine. In a big house it might be a whole room. In a student apartment it's a shelf above the desk. In a lot of kitchens it's a little alcove near the stove, with a picture of Krishna leaning against the spice jars and a lamp that's been lit every morning for as long as anyone remembers. It's called the mandir, the temple, or the puja room, even when it's only a shelf. Nobody needs permission to make one. And a simple one can come down to five things.
screen: `A ROOM, OR A SHELF.` → `KRISHNA BY THE SPICE JARS.` → `IT COMES DOWN TO FIVE THINGS.`

segments.voice: One: an image. A small statue, called a murti, or a picture. Of your ishta, the face you're drawn to, or Ganesha, or the family's deity. Many Hindus understand the image as a place where the divine is present, and treat it like an honored guest. Others see it as a focus for the mind. Both are held. Two: a lamp. A small clay or brass lamp, with oil or ghee and a cotton wick. Light is offered, and tomorrow the lamp gets a whole day. Three: a flower. Fresh, if you can. Something beautiful, given away, that won't last. Four: a bell. A small hand bell, rung at the start of puja, to call the attention of the divine, many say, and your own. Five: water. A small cup or pot of clean water, offered, sipped, sprinkled. Nothing on that list is expensive. That's the point: the care counts, not the cost. Where does it go? Traditions offer guidance. Many prefer the image facing east or west, with you facing it, and a spot that's clean and a little apart, not in the bathroom or under the stairs. But a home shrine grows out of the life you actually have. A clean shelf you pass every morning is better than a perfect room you never enter. This week you'll build yours, piece by piece. Today, just the corner. A corner that's yours.
screen: `AN IMAGE — THE HONORED GUEST.` · `A LAMP, A FLOWER.` · `A BELL, AND WATER.` · `NOTHING HERE IS EXPENSIVE.` · then, large: `A CORNER THAT'S YOURS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: assemble. Look around where you are, and choose a place. A shelf, the corner of a dresser, a windowsill. Clear it. Wipe it with your hand if nothing else. Now gather what you have. An image or a picture that means something to you. A candle or a tea light for a lamp. A flower, or a leaf from outside. Anything that rings, even a spoon on a glass. A small cup of water. Set them down, slowly. If you can't do it right now, picture exactly where it will go. Then sit in front of it, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Five objects. An image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, and water: the whole home shrine, in five simple things.
Your line: a corner that's yours. Today, pass your corner once on purpose, and leave one fresh thing there: a flower, a leaf, a cup of clean water. Day one hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes keep a small shrine, from a whole puja room to a kitchen shelf, with an image or picture of the family's deities, a lamp, flowers, a bell and water, where daily puja is offered.

myth: a home shrine has to be a whole room

nothing on the simple shelf needs to be expensive

fork.setup: you want to make a home shrine, but you live in a tiny apartment with no spare room. what do you do?
options: wait until you have a bigger place.
clear one shelf you pass every morning.
put it somewhere hidden, like under the stairs.
fork.reveal: a clean shelf you pass every morning is better than a perfect room you never enter. many traditions avoid spots like under the stairs.

original.note: Sanskrit: form, embodiment; the image at the center of a shrine.

trapdoor: what you thought: a shrine is a statue and some decorations.
what it means: a corner of your own, with five simple things: an image, a lamp, a flower, a bell, water.

what a scholar hears: the murti understood by many as a place of presence after consecration (prana pratishtha); the classic upacharas, the offerings of puja, of which these five are a simple home set, not the classical list.

sources.ref: home shrine and puja practice (murti, lamp, flowers, bell, water)

notes: The five objects follow the outline index (image, lamp, flower, bell, water). The classical panchopachara (five offerings) is usually sandalwood paste, flower, incense, lamp and food, which differs; the script doesn't claim these five are a traditional set. Keeper may wish to mention it.

Reviewer fix: softened 'almost any Hindu home' / 'most Hindu homes' to 'many', and 'almost all of them come down to five things' to 'a simple one can come down to five things', since shrine practice varies widely.
Gita 9.26 paraphrased (no pre-1929 wording quoted). Confirm.
Placement guidance (east or west facing; avoiding bathrooms and under stairs) reflects common Vastu-influenced advice; varies. Confirm.
'Anything that rings, even a spoon on a glass' as a substitute for a bell; Keeper may prefer different wording.
Murti understood as presence (after prana pratishtha) or as a focus for the mind: both views given. Confirm.
